text.en: Raju heard that the Sun makes its energy by fusing hydrogen. "Nuclear energy powers the stars," said his teacher.

Radioactivity is spontaneous decay of unstable atomic nuclei, discovered by Henri Becquerel while studying uranium salts. The nucleus before decay is the parent. A nucleus produced by decay is called a daughter nucleus. Activity measures decays per second. The SI unit is the becquerel and an older unit is the curie.
Alpha, beta and gamma radiation have different properties. Fission splits a heavy nucleus, while fusion joins light nuclei. Fusion powers the Sun, and controlled fission supplies heat that a nuclear power station can use to generate electricity.
Radioisotopes have applications in medicine, research and industry. Radiation protection is part of those applications because ionising radiation can affect living tissue.
Radioactivity is the spontaneous emission of radiation by unstable atomic nuclei. Henri Becquerel discovered it while studying uranium salts.
Some radioactive isotopes occur naturally and others are produced in controlled scientific settings. Once an unstable nucleus exists, its decay is spontaneous.
The disintegrating nucleus is the parent and the one produced is the daughter.
The curie, 3.7 x 10^10 disintegrations per second, and the becquerel are the units.
Alpha and beta radiation consist of particles. Gamma radiation is electromagnetic. Each kind of decay can be described by tracking the changes in the nucleus.
In nuclear fission, a heavy nucleus splits into smaller nuclei and releases energy. Nuclear power stations can use energy from controlled fission to generate electricity.
Nuclear fusion joins light nuclei into a heavier nucleus. Energy released by fusion helps the Sun and other stars shine.
Radioisotopes have applications in medicine, research and industry. Trained professionals control and monitor exposure to ionising radiation.
Protons give it a positive charge. The number of protons fixes which element the atom belongs to.

board.text: A nucleus contains protons and usually neutrons

text.en: Two isotopes of an element have the same proton count and different neutron counts. Some isotopes are stable and others can decay.
An unstable nucleus can release particles or energy. A chemical reaction rearranges electrons and bonds, while nuclear decay changes the nucleus itself.
You cannot say exactly when one particular nucleus will decay. The behaviour of a large collection follows a predictable statistical pattern.
The original nucleus is called the parent. The resulting nucleus is called the daughter and may itself be stable or unstable.

board.text: A daughter nucleus is a result, not a second parent

text.en: An alpha particle contains two protons and two neutrons. When it leaves, the parent nucleus loses those four particles.
During beta-minus decay, the nucleus emits an electron. This is a nuclear process, distinct from removing an outer electron in chemistry.

board.text: A beta-minus particle is an electron

text.en: Gamma radiation carries energy without carrying protons or neutrons. Emitting it can leave the same element and isotope in a lower-energy state.
Alpha, beta and gamma can transfer enough energy to remove electrons from atoms. Ionisation can affect matter, including living tissue.
If a sample has activity forty becquerels, it averages forty decays each second. The becquerel tells us the decay rate.
Activity describes how often nuclei decay. Dose relates to energy absorbed and possible effects of exposure, so activity alone does not tell you a person’s dose.

board.text: Activity and dose measure different things

text.en: After one half-life, about half the original radioactive nuclei remain. After another half-life, half of the remaining nuclei are left.

board.text: A half-life describes a population of nuclei

text.en: In a model with eighty nuclei, one half-life leaves about forty. The next leaves about twenty, which is one quarter of the starting count.

board.text: Half of the remainder is not half of the original

text.en: A heavy nucleus separates into smaller nuclei and energy is released. The word fission describes the change in the nucleus.
Light nuclei can join and form a heavier nucleus. Under the conditions in stars, fusion can release energy.
Fusion in the Sun’s core releases energy. That energy eventually reaches the surface and some travels to Earth as sunlight.

board.text: The Sun gives a familiar fusion example

text.en: Controlled nuclear fission releases heat. A power station uses that heat to produce electricity through energy conversion.

board.text: A nuclear station converts heat into electricity

text.en: Burning rearranges atoms in a chemical reaction. Fission and fusion change atomic nuclei.

board.text: Fission and fusion are different from burning

text.en: In hospitals, trained teams use some radioisotopes to image body processes or for treatment. The isotope and exposure are selected for the purpose.
Researchers can use known decay patterns when dating suitable materials. The method chosen depends on the material and the period being studied.
Facilities monitor and limit exposure. Students can study radiation using diagrams and models without handling radioactive sources.

board.text: Radiation devices belong under professional control

text.en: To state a decay rate, use becquerels. To describe a reduction in remaining parent nuclei, use half-life. To classify a nuclear change, ask what happens to the nucleus.

The sample averages 25 decays per second.

problem.en: A model starts with 80 parent nuclei. Estimate how many remain after two half-lives.

text.en: After one half-life, about 40 remain.

why.en: This is half of the starting number.

text.en: After the second half-life, about 20 remain.

why.en: Each interval halves the number that remained at its start.

The resulting energy helps power sunlight.
